title: The Naira Is Not Your Enemy. Inflation Is.
excerpt: Everyone blames the exchange rate. The quieter problem is what your money loses while it sits still.
content:
Ask almost anyone in Lagos why saving money feels pointless, and you will hear the same answer: the naira. The exchange rate gets the blame for everything. But the exchange rate is only the headline. The quieter problem, the one that empties accounts while nobody is watching, is inflation.

Think of your savings account as a bucket. Every month you pour a little more water in. That feels like progress, because the water line keeps rising. What you cannot see is the small hole in the bottom. Inflation is that hole. You are pouring faster than you are losing, so the bucket still fills, and you tell yourself the plan is working. Then one day you go to buy something you could afford two years ago, and the money is not enough.

What inflation actually does to a salary

Inflation is not an abstract number announced by the National Bureau of Statistics. It is the difference between what your salary bought last year and what it buys today.

Say you earn 500,000 naira a month and you got no raise this year. If prices rose 25 percent over that period, you did not simply stay flat. You took a pay cut. Your salary now buys roughly what 400,000 naira bought twelve months ago. Nobody sent you a letter about it. No manager sat you down. It happened quietly, in the price of rice, transport, school fees and rent.

This is why people who are technically earning more each year still feel poorer. They are comparing the number on the payslip instead of comparing what the number can do.

Why a savings account is not saving

Here is the part that stings. A regular savings account in Nigeria pays a small amount of interest. If that interest is well below the inflation rate, then leaving money there is not a neutral decision. It is a slow, guaranteed loss.

Money in a low interest account during high inflation is not sitting still. It is shrinking politely.

That does not mean savings accounts are useless. They are the right home for your emergency fund, the three to six months of expenses you might need at short notice. Liquidity is worth paying for. The mistake is treating a savings account as a wealth building tool when its actual job is to be boring and available.

The real return test

Before you put money anywhere, run one simple test. Take the return the product promises, and subtract the inflation rate. What is left is your real return. That is the only number that matters, because that is the number that decides whether your money is growing or quietly dying.

  • An investment paying 10 percent while inflation runs at 25 percent is losing you 15 percent a year in real terms.
  • An investment paying 30 percent in the same conditions is gaining you 5 percent.
  • Cash under the mattress paying nothing is losing the full inflation rate.

Most financial products are advertised using the first number and never the second. Learning to do that subtraction in your head is one of the highest value skills you can build.

Three moves that actually help

Separate your money by job. Emergency money belongs somewhere safe and instantly reachable, and you should accept that it will lose a little value. Long term money has a different job, and it needs to be somewhere with a real chance of beating inflation. Mixing the two is how people end up either broke in an emergency or poor in retirement.

Own things, not just currency. Currency is a claim on value. Assets are value. Shares in real companies, property that produces rent, and instruments tied to harder currencies all behave differently from cash when local prices climb. You do not need to pick perfectly. You need to stop holding everything in the one asset that is guaranteed to weaken.

Increase what you earn, not only what you keep. There is a floor to how much you can cut. There is no ceiling on what you can earn. A raise, a second income, or a skill that pays in a stronger currency will usually outrun any amount of careful budgeting. Budgeting protects the money you have. Earning changes the game.

The point

The naira is a currency. It moves for reasons far outside your control, and being angry at it changes nothing. Inflation, on the other hand, is a force you can plan around once you can see it clearly.

Stop asking whether your money is growing. Start asking whether it is growing faster than prices are rising. That single change in question will reshape every financial decision you make from here.
author: Fisayo Adeyemi
